title: A Paper Taped to a Door Counted as Legal Notice
description:
In 1975 a deputy sheriff went to an apartment door in a Louisville public housing project, found nobody home, and fixed a court paper to the outside of the door. Under Kentucky law that was service. The notice carried the time and place the court would meet, and the case would go ahead whether or not anyone inside ever read a word of it.

The tenants were Linnie Lindsey, Barbara Hodgens and Pamela Ray. Their landlord was the Housing Authority of Louisville, a government body rather than a private owner, and the proceeding was a forcible entry and detainer action, the summary process used to take possession back quickly. The opinion gives their three names and a housing project and almost nothing else: no ages, no jobs, no arrears, no account of what they were supposed to have done.

They said they never saw the posted summonses, and that they learned of the proceedings only when writs of possession arrived, after default judgments had been entered and after their opportunity for appeal had lapsed. That is their account, not a finding. The case was decided on cross-motions for summary judgment and nobody ever tested it, and the Court itself kept the distance: appellees claim to have suffered precisely such a failure of actual notice.

The whole evidentiary record was the depositions of the process servers. Children pulled the writs off doors, they said, so they had been told to put the papers up high. In a good percentage of visits nobody was home, and posting followed forthwith, with no provision for even a second attempt at a time of day when the tenant was more likely to be in. The district court ruled for the sheriff on the authority of a 1909 case while conceding in the same breath that conditions had changed. The Sixth Circuit reversed and overruled its own precedent.

On 17 May 1982 the Supreme Court affirmed. Justice Brennan began by defending the practice: short of personal service, posting notice on the door of a person's home would, in many or perhaps most instances, be a singularly appropriate and effective way of reaching someone. Then the turn. In the circumstances of this case it was not, because in a significant number of instances the notice never reached the tenant and, as the process servers were well aware, papers posted in that area were not infrequently removed before they could have their intended effect. What was at stake was named plainly: a significant interest in property, the right to continued residence in their homes.

The part that usually gets lost is what the Court refused to do. It did not ban posting; it held only that posted notice under section 454.030 was constitutionally inadequate. It did not order Kentucky to use the mail, because it is not our responsibility to prescribe the form of service, and it said only that posting accompanied by mail is constitutionally preferable to posting alone. It did not hand the three tenants their apartments back either: it affirmed a judgment that had reversed a grant of summary judgment and remanded the case for further proceedings. What became of Linnie Lindsey, Barbara Hodgens and Pamela Ray after that is not in the opinion, and this film does not say.

Three Justices dissented. Justice O'Connor, joined by the Chief Justice and Justice Rehnquist, wrote that the Court had made a constitutional rule out of the scant and conflicting testimony of a handful of process servers, with no evidence in the record about the speed or reliability of the mails, and had overturned the work of the Kentucky legislature and, by implication, at least ten other states. Unattended mailboxes, she added, are subject to plunder by thieves, while posting at least gives assurance that the notice has got as far as the tenant's door. The opinion prints no vote.

Some imagery in this film is AI-assisted and symbolic; no real-person likeness is shown, and no eviction is depicted.
Greene v. Lindsey, 456 U.S. 444 (1982).
